Urothelium.description: The urothelium is the specialised lining of the bladder. It is a transitional epithelium that forms a tight barrier, so urine does not soak into the wall. Basal cells on the basement membrane regenerate the lining, intermediate cells sit above them, and large umbrella cells cover the surface, where uroplakin plaques make the membrane almost impermeable to urine.
clinical: Most bladder cancers begin in the urothelium, and urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma is the most common type. Painless blood in the urine (haematuria) is the most common early sign and always needs investigation.
The chemotherapy drug cyclophosphamide is broken down into acrolein, which injures the urothelium and can cause bleeding inflammation of the bladder (haemorrhagic cystitis).

Umbrella cell envelopes.description: Umbrella cells are the large, dome-shaped cells that form the surface layer of the urothelium, facing the urine. As the bladder fills, membrane stored inside them is added to the surface, so the surface can expand as the bladder stretches.
clinical: Umbrella cells shed into the urine can be examined under the microscope (urine cytology), which is one way doctors look for bladder cancer.

Umbrella cell contents.description: Umbrella cells often have large nuclei, and many contain two (binucleate). This is normal in the surface layer and is not a sign of cancer. Their upper cytoplasm holds fusiform vesicles that store uroplakin-rich membrane, which is delivered to the surface when the bladder fills.
clinical: Binucleate umbrella cells are normal, but enlarged, irregular nuclei in cells shed into the urine can point to urothelial carcinoma and need expert review.

Lamina propria.description: The lamina propria is the connective-tissue layer directly beneath the urothelium. It holds a dense suburothelial capillary plexus with small arterioles and venules, because the urothelium has no blood vessels of its own and is nourished by diffusion from this bed.
clinical: Bladder cancers are staged by how deep they grow. Tumours that reach the lamina propria (stage T1) but not the detrusor muscle are non-muscle-invasive and are usually removed by transurethral resection.

Detrusor muscle.description: The detrusor is the thick smooth-muscle wall of the bladder. Its fibres form one interlaced meshwork, so the whole bladder contracts together to empty (voiding), under parasympathetic control. Its inner, middle and outer layers are only clearly separate near the bladder neck.
clinical: Involuntary detrusor contractions cause sudden urgency, frequent urination and sometimes leaking (urge incontinence).
If the nerves that drive the detrusor are damaged, for example by spinal cord injury or diabetes, the muscle may fail to contract, so the bladder cannot empty fully (urinary retention).

Adventitia & serosa.description: The outer coat of the bladder is adventitia, a connective-tissue sheath that holds fat, vessels and nerves and fixes the bladder to the pelvic walls. The dome (upper surface) is instead covered by serosa, which is peritoneum, so that surface borders the peritoneal cavity.
clinical: A full bladder hit on its dome, for example in a blow to the lower abdomen, can rupture into the peritoneal cavity and spill urine into the abdomen. Pelvic fractures more often tear the bladder outside the peritoneum.
Operations on the prostate, rectum or pelvis can damage the nerves that control the bladder, causing difficulty emptying or leaking.

parts.description: Basal cells are the small, rounded cells that form the deepest layer of the urothelium, resting directly on the basement membrane. They act as the stem cells of the lining, dividing to replace the intermediate and umbrella cells above them. In a section, look for a single row of small, darkly stained nuclei along the base of the epithelium.

Intermediate cells are the middle layers of the urothelium, lying between the basal cells below and the large umbrella cells at the surface. They are pear-shaped or polygonal, and their layers flatten and thin as the bladder fills, so the middle zone is several cells deep when the bladder is empty and only a few cells deep when it is stretched. In a section, they fill the space between the basal row and the surface layer.

Uroplakin plaques are rigid patches of membrane proteins on the apical (luminal) surface of umbrella cells, the side that faces the urine. They form an almost impermeable barrier that stops urine and its solutes leaking into the wall, and flexible hinge regions between the plaques let the membrane fold as the bladder fills. Electron microscopy is needed to see the plaque pattern itself, where the plaques appear as thick membrane patches arranged in hexagonal arrays.

The urothelial basement membrane is the thin sheet of extracellular matrix that separates the basal cells of the urothelium from the lamina propria below. It anchors the lining to the connective tissue and lets nutrients diffuse from the capillaries up to the basal cells, because the urothelium itself has no blood vessels. In a section, it appears as a thin, pink line under the basal cells on H&E, and it stains strongly magenta with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS).

Lamina propria arterioles are the small arteries and arterioles that run through the lamina propria beneath the urothelium, carrying blood to the capillary network. Their walls contain a layer of smooth muscle that lets them adjust blood flow, and they branch into the suburothelial capillaries. In a section, look for small round vessels with a thicker muscular wall than the nearby venules and a small lumen, usually containing red blood cells.

The suburothelial capillary plexus is the dense network of thin-walled capillaries lying just beneath the urothelium, in the upper lamina propria. It receives blood from the arterioles and drains into the venules, and it supplies the urothelium by diffusion, since the lining itself has no blood vessels. In a section, look for many small capillaries packed close beneath the basal surface of the lining, each with a wall of flat endothelial cells.

Lamina propria venules are the small, thin-walled veins of the lamina propria that collect blood from the suburothelial capillary plexus and carry it onward to the larger veins of the bladder wall. Their walls contain much less smooth muscle than the arterioles beside them. In a section, look for small vessels with a wide, often irregular lumen and a thin wall, which may contain red blood cells.

The muscularis mucosae is a thin, patchy layer of smooth muscle at the deep edge of the lamina propria, separating it from the detrusor below. In the bladder it is discontinuous, usually best developed near the bladder neck and trigone, and only patchy over the rest of the wall. In a section, look for small bundles of smooth muscle cells in this position, with gaps where the layer is missing.

The inner longitudinal detrusor is the innermost of the three layers of the bladder's thick smooth-muscle wall, the detrusor, and its bundles run lengthwise just beneath the lamina propria. Together with the middle circular and outer longitudinal layers, it contracts to empty the bladder during voiding. In a section, the layers are most clearly separate near the bladder neck, and elsewhere they blend into one meshwork that is hard to divide into layers.

The middle circular detrusor is the central layer of the bladder's smooth-muscle wall, made of bundles that run around the bladder rather than along it. Lying between the inner and outer longitudinal layers, it narrows the bladder cavity when it contracts and helps push urine out during voiding. In a section, its bundles are often cut in cross-section, but the boundaries with the neighbouring layers are blurred.

The outer longitudinal detrusor is the outermost layer of the bladder's smooth-muscle wall, lying just beneath the adventitia or serosa, with bundles that run lengthwise over the bladder. It shortens the bladder together with the other layers and helps to empty it during voiding. In a section, it appears as the outer band of smooth muscle, usually cut obliquely or lengthwise, and it blends into the middle layer.

The interlacing (oblique) bundles are smooth-muscle fibres that run diagonally between the longitudinal and circular layers of the detrusor, linking them into one meshwork. Because they cross the layers, they help the whole wall contract together rather than in separate sheets. In a section, they show as smooth-muscle bundles cut at angles, which is why the boundaries between the layers look blurred.

Interfascicular connective tissue is the collagen and elastic-fibre matrix that lies between the bundles (fascicles) of detrusor smooth muscle and holds them together. It carries the small blood vessels and nerve fibres that supply the muscle. In a section, it shows as pale pink strands of collagen between the darker smooth-muscle bundles on H&E, and as dark, wavy elastic fibres on elastic stains.

The serosa is the thin outer covering of the bladder dome, the upper surface of the bladder. It is visceral peritoneum: a single layer of flat mesothelial cells on a thin connective-tissue layer, which makes the surface smooth and moist so that it slides freely against neighbouring bowel. In a section, the serosa is recognised by its flat surface cells, unlike the looser connective tissue of the adventitia on the rest of the wall.

The adventitia is the outer connective-tissue coat of the bladder, covering the wall wherever it is not covered by peritoneum. It is loose connective tissue that holds the fat, blood vessels and nerves supplying the wall, and it fixes the bladder to the surrounding pelvic structures. In a section, look for a loose, pale collagen layer with fat cells and vessels scattered through it, lying outside the thick smooth-muscle detrusor.

Perivesical fat is the layer of adipose tissue that surrounds the bladder outside its outer coat, filling the space between the bladder and the pelvic walls. It cushions the bladder, allows it to expand as it fills, and carries the vessels and nerves that run to the wall. In a section, it appears as clusters of fat cells with large clear cytoplasm and their nuclei pushed to the edge, with capillaries between them.

The vesical arteries are the branches that supply the bladder wall, and the superior and inferior vesical arteries arise from the internal iliac arteries. They run in the adventitia and send branches through the detrusor and into the mucosa. In a section or dissection, they are thick-walled muscular arteries with round lumens, lying among the fat and the veins of the outer coat.

The vesical veins form the vesical venous plexus, a network of thin-walled veins in the adventitia around the base and sides of the bladder. The plexus drains into the internal iliac veins and joins the prostatic venous plexus in men and the vaginal venous plexus in women. In a section, these veins are thin-walled, with wide and often collapsed lumens, and they lie beside the thicker-walled arteries.

The autonomic nerves of the bladder are bundles of nerve fibres in its wall that control filling and emptying. Parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) drive contraction and voiding, while sympathetic fibres from the hypogastric nerves (T10-L2) relax the detrusor. Small intramural ganglia, which are clusters of nerve cell bodies, lie among the bundles, and in a section they show as groups of large neurons with round nuclei and prominent nucleoli.

Umbrella cell nuclei are the large nuclei of the surface cells of the urothelium, the cells that face the urine. Many umbrella cells are binucleate, with two nuclei, or polyploid, with more than the usual number of chromosome sets, and this is normal for them. Such large nuclei should not be confused with cancer cells in a biopsy or urine sample, so in a section look for big, rounded nuclei in the outermost layer.

Fusiform vesicles are spindle-shaped membrane sacs in the upper cytoplasm of umbrella cells, just beneath the apical surface, that store uroplakin-rich membrane. When the bladder fills, these vesicles fuse with the apical membrane and add membrane to the surface, so the lining can stretch; when the bladder empties, the membrane is taken back into the cell. They are seen only with electron microscopy, as elongated membrane-bound vesicles grouped under the surface.
